description:
Hello from Uruguay! 🇺🇾🚀

We are Nova, a team of students from Santa Elena School in Uruguay, excited to participate in the NASA Space Apps Challenge! 🌎✨
summary: Our project proposes an intelligent fire-safety platform for spacecraft and future lunar and Martian habitats. In microgravity there is no buoyancy or natural convection, so flames become spherical, pale blue and slow-burning, and they produce no rising smoke column. As a result, conventional smoke detectors may fail or react too late, and toxic gases such as carbon monoxide can build up near the ignition point. Future Artemis lunar bases and Mars habitats will also use lower pressures and higher oxygen levels, which make materials ignite faster and with less energy. Our solution combines a vector database of fire experiment data, an AI engine that answers questions in natural language, a risk classification module for cabin materials, and automated emergency protocols. Together, these tools help crews and mission designers understand fire risk quickly and respond safely when astronauts cannot simply leave the spacecraft.
details:
What it does and how it works. The platform has four connected modules:

  1. Vector database: indexes technical reports, high-speed video of flame experiments, and data from thermal and gas sensors, so all information about how materials burn in space is stored in one searchable place.
  2. AI engine: lets users ask questions in natural language (for example, “How fast does this fabric burn at 34% oxygen?”) and returns instant summaries about heat release rate and extinction time for each material.
  3. Risk classification module: ranks the materials found inside each module from lowest to highest risk, depending on the habitat’s pressure and oxygen conditions.
  4. Automated emergency protocols: recommends immediate actions when an alert is triggered, such as selectively shutting down ventilation fans to cut off the oxygen supply without spreading toxic gases through the cabin.
    Benefits and intended impact. It turns scattered scientific data into fast, practical decisions. It can help engineers choose safer materials before a mission and help crews react correctly in the first critical seconds of a fire.

Factors we considered. How fire physics changes without gravity (diffusion instead of convection), why Earth-based detectors fail in space, the build-up of toxic combustion gases, and the special atmospheres planned for the Moon and Mars (lower pressure, higher oxygen).

Creativity. Instead of designing a new sensor, we focused on connecting knowledge: using AI to make decades of space fire research usable in real time, adapted to each habitat’s conditions.

Tools used. The project was researched and presented using Canva.
